activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
story:
Alexander set the microscope on the picnic table and peered into the eyepiece. Nothing. A gray smear, that was all, and he had promised Mr. Ross the labeled drawing by tomorrow morning.

"Any cells yet?" Himmat asked, leaning over his shoulder.

"Any cells? I can't even find the slide. It's like staring into a jar of fog." Alexander had twisted the biggest lens, the one marked 40x, right down until it nearly touched the glass, because the biggest lens had to show the most. That was obvious. Except the obvious was a purple blur.

Pablo held the onion chunk at arm's length. "This thing is starting to smell toxic. My eyes are watering from two feet away."

"It's an onion, not a weapon." Alexander turned the focus knob again, a hair's width at a time. The blur swam, bent like light through a water glass, and refused to become anything.

"Give it here." Himmat took over, clicked the smallest lens into place, the one marked 4x, and started turning.

"That's the weakest one," Alexander said. "Why bother?"

"Because you find them first, then zoom. You start on the little lens, get the cells in focus, then switch up to the bigger ones."

Alexander stared at him. "How do you know that?"

Himmat grinned. "My cousin got an eye infection last spring and couldn't do his lab, so the teacher let me do it twice. First time I did exactly what you're doing. Blur city."

"Blur city," Pablo repeated solemnly, like it was a place with a mayor.

Himmat cranked the small lens down. "There. Look." Alexander bent to the eyepiece and there they were, rows of brick-shaped cells, neat as a tile floor, each with a dark dot floating inside. He held his breath and clicked to the next lens, the 10x, careful not to bump the table. The cells swelled larger. One more click to the 40x and the nucleus filled the view like a moon.

"Get the pencil," he said. "Cell wall, membrane, nucleus, all of it. I can even see the wall's double edge."

Pablo drew fast while Alexander called out shapes, and Himmat guarded the microscope like a goalie. When the drawing was done, Alexander slid the slide out and noticed the thin skin had dried at the edge, curled like burnt paper.

"Next time," Pablo said, sniffling, "somebody else cuts the onion. I'm going to smell like a haunted kitchen."

"Deal," Alexander said, and propped the drawing against the lemonade pitcher where the afternoon light hit it, every label crisp and clear.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
story:
The lights went out just after seven, and Brody's first thought was the freezer. He found the candles in the hall closet, set three of them on the coffee table, and got the flashlight from the kitchen drawer even though they didn't need it yet. His mother settled onto the couch with a blanket, and his little sister dragged her pillows into the living room because she didn't like being alone in the dark. The candles made the room feel smaller and warmer at the same time, and the quiet outside seemed to cooperate with the quiet inside, like the whole street had agreed to hush.

"Don't open the freezer," his mother said when Brody wandered toward the kitchen. "Every time you open it, the cold gets out."

"I know," he said. "I'm not opening it. I'm just thinking." He had read something once, in a pamphlet from the grocery store that he'd kept for no reason he could remember. It had said that thawed freezer food could be safely refrozen if it still contained ice crystals, or if it was at forty degrees Fahrenheit or below, which was four degrees Celsius. He'd thought it was strange that the pamphlet gave both scales, but now he was glad, because their fridge thermometer only showed Celsius.

Isla texted him from down the street: "power out there too? we're grilling everything before it spoils lol." Brody typed back that they were keeping the freezer shut and waiting. Rohan sent a single question mark, and then, "my dad says throw everything out tomorrow." That felt arbitrary to Brody, throwing out food without checking anything first. There was a rule, and rules were better than guesses.

The lights came back at nine twenty. The furnace hummed, the sister whooped, and Brody went straight to the freezer with the thermometer and the bag of peas. He pressed his finger against the plastic and felt the small hard bumps shifting inside, each one distinct, like cold gravel. Ice crystals. He wedged the thermometer between the bags and waited, watching the numbers instead of the clock, until it settled at three degrees Celsius, which was below four.

"Still frozen," he called into the living room. "The peas have ice crystals, and it's three degrees in here. The rule says food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals or if it's at forty degrees Fahrenheit, which is four Celsius. We're under both. We don't have to throw anything out."

His mother came and looked over his shoulder at the thermometer, then at the bag in his hands. "Where did you learn that?"

"A pamphlet," Brody said. "I kept it." He put the peas back on the shelf, shut the door, and blew out the last candle.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out, so slow breathing with long out-breaths helps the heart settle.
story:
Zack had one week before the geography bee, and his heart already knew it. It hammered during lunch, hammered during practice questions, and hammered hardest when Ms. Pérez posted the bracket on the classroom wall with his name in the second row. Austen found him staring at it. "You look like you're going to pass out," Austen said. "I'm not going to pass out," Zack said, though his hands were cold and his stomach felt like it had swallowed a stone.

That night he lay awake and thought about the summer, when his cousin had stayed with them for a month while her family waited for paperwork. She was a refugee, his mom had explained, a family that had to leave their home and hadn't found a new one yet. Zack remembered watching her sit very still on the porch doing something strange: breathing out through puckered lips, slowly, like she was cooling soup. He'd asked why. She'd said her mother taught her, back when things were bad, that the heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out. He'd shrugged and gone back to his bike. Now, in the dark, he wondered if he should have paid more attention.

The next day he tested it in science class. Under the desk, where Lawrence couldn't see, he put two fingers on his wrist and breathed normally. On each breath in, the beat under his fingers quickened, a little drum rolling faster. On each breath out, it slowed again. It happened every single time, like a rule the heart followed without asking him. He tried stretching the out-breath longer than the in-breath, counting to six out, and the beat stretched out too, settling like a dog told to lie down.

He cornered Lawrence at the water fountain. "Breathe in while I time you, then out for longer, and feel your pulse." Lawrence rolled his eyes but did it, fingers on his own wrist, counting. "Whoa," Lawrence said. "It speeds up when I breathe in and slows down when I breathe out. That's so weird." "It's not weird, it's a thing," Zack said, though until yesterday he hadn't known it was a thing at all.

The problem was nighttime. The breathing calmed his heart, but his brain kept running the bee like a movie he couldn't turn off. He remembered what his cousin had done after the porch: the same bedtime every night, lights low, no screens, the same three slow breaths before sleep. He'd thought it was boring then, a temporary ritual for a temporary life. Now he tried it himself. Phone charging in the hallway. Lights off at nine-thirty. Six counts out, again and again. He slept through the night for the first time in a week.

The morning of the bee, Ms. Pérez called the contestants to the front. Zack's heart started its old drumroll as he walked up. He breathed in for four, out for six, in for four, out for six, quietly so no one would notice. The pounding loosened its grip. Maybe it was the breathing, or maybe it was the sleeping, or maybe both. He couldn't tell which, and he decided that was okay.

The first question was about the longest river in South America, which he knew cold. His hand hovered over the buzzer. Breathe out, press. "The Amazon," he said, and the little light on his podium glowed green.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
story:
Sophia had exactly forty minutes of coding club left, and her program still thought that 9 was prime. She glared at the screen, then at her friend Ryan, who was leaning over her shoulder eating pretzels with his mouth open.

"Nine is not prime," she said. "It's 3 times 3. My code is lying to me."

"Your code can't lie," Ryan said. "It only does what you tell it. So basically you told it to be wrong."

"That's the most annoying true thing you've ever said."

Her program was supposed to ask for a number, then print whether it was prime, meaning nothing divided it except 1 and itself. She'd written a loop that tested divisors, and she was pretty sure the bug hid somewhere in the part where the loop decided to stop. The problem was she couldn't see the loop running. She could only see its results, like footprints in snow. So she tried an experiment: she made the program print every divisor it tested, right there on the screen.

"Two, then four, then it stops," she said. "It never tests 3."

Ryan crunched a pretzel. "Why does it skip 3?"

Sophia read her own line of code out loud. "Because it goes up by two. I thought I was being clever, starting at 2 and jumping the even numbers." She'd have to salvage the clever part and rebuild the rest. She changed the loop so it tested every number, and suddenly the program announced, correctly, that 9 was not prime. She fed it 7, then 11, then 97, and it got every one right.

Loik slid his chair over from the next table, holding a dusty blue book he'd pulled off Ms. Rivera's shelf. "You two are arguing about primes? Look at this. Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers."

"There's a whole book about them?" Ryan said.

"Old book," Loik said. "Like, older than the gym floor old."

Ryan set down his pretzels, which for Ryan was a serious gesture. "Wait. Infinitely many? I was going to find the biggest prime and name it after myself. Primus Ryanicus."

"You'd have needed a bigger computer," Sophia said. "And a longer life. And more snacks."

Loik grinned. "There is no biggest one. That's the whole point."

Sophia looked at her little program, then at the ancient book, then at her program again. Her code checked one number at a time, and it would happily do that forever if you kept typing numbers in. It was a tiny hinge that swung open onto something enormous. Somewhere out there, past every number she could ever test, more primes kept going, and going, and going, like a hallway with no far wall.

Ms. Rivera walked by and tapped the top of Sophia's monitor. "Ten minutes to save your work, everyone."

Sophia typed one more test into her program, mostly because she wanted to watch it answer.

"Is 101 prime?" she asked the screen.

It printed its answer before she finished her pretzel, and she turned to Ryan and said, "Primus Ryanicus has been canceled."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
story:
The parking lot of the gurdwara was a field of shoes, and Elliot stood at the edge of it with his sneakers still on, watching. Grandfathers in slippers, toddlers in light-up sneakers, his cousin Keiran hopping on one foot while pulling off a boot. Every single person was leaving their shoes outside, and every single adult was tying something over their head before passing through the doors. Elliot counted. Eleven people in, eleven shoes off, eleven heads covered. Was it a family rule, a rule of the building, or something everyone just knew except him?

He tested his first idea quietly. He kept his shoes on and walked toward the entrance, half expecting an alarm. A man by the door only pointed at a shelf of scarves and then at Elliot's feet, not angry, just pointing. So it wasn't a family rule. Was it a rule for this place only, or did other places like this have the same one? He filed the question away and pulled off his sneakers.

Inside, Keiran handed him a thin orange scarf. "You have to cover your head here," Keiran said. "Everyone does." Elliot looped it the way he'd seen his aunt do it, badly, and it slid off immediately, which made a little girl in the next row laugh so hard she had to exhale and start over. Her grandmother told a short anecdote about Keiran once wearing a bath towel as a turban because he couldn't find a scarf, and Keiran went pink to his ears.

In the langar hall afterward, rows of people sat on the floor eating dal and roti, and nobody's feet were bare because nobody's shoes were on the floor either. That was the piece Elliot had been missing. He leaned toward his cousin Beatrice, who was visiting with her class that morning. "Do mosques do the shoe thing too?" he asked. Beatrice nodded. "And Hindu temples. Gurdwaras, mosques, temples, lots of them. Shoes off at all of them, and heads covered at the gurdwara especially."

"So it's like a pattern," Elliot said, and something clicked into place, a hidden rule you could only see by watching what everyone did. He pulled out his phone under the table and typed a message to his mother, who was arriving late from work: "Take off your shoes before the doors and grab a scarf from the shelf on the left. Trust me. Count them yourself if you want."

Twenty minutes later his mother appeared in the doorway, shoes already in one hand, a green scarf knotted on her head like she'd done it a hundred times. She caught his eye across the hall and raised her shoe at him like a trophy.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: "Agenda" is a Latin word meaning "things to be done," and a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed.
story:
The first meeting of the Maple Street Rocket Club was supposed to last one hour, and it vanished into a bowl of pretzels. Isaak talked about a documentary about satellites. Sofie argued that the club mascot should be a penguin. By the time anyone looked at the clock, forty minutes had gone to snacks and nothing had been decided, and Mr. Nowak, Isaak's neighbour, had already stuck a note through the letterbox saying the community fair wanted the club's plan by Friday or the club couldn't have a table. Tristan read the note twice, then announced that they needed an agenda.

"You mean like a fancy to-do list?" Isaak asked, still holding the pretzel bowl.

Sofie, who read dictionaries for fun, straightened up. "Agenda is a Latin word meaning things to be done," she said. "And a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they'll be discussed."

That gave Tristan an idea he wanted to test. He wrote four items on a sheet of paper: mascot vote, rocket design, budget, fair plan. "We follow the order," he said. "Nobody can jump ahead, not even me." He even allocated time, ten minutes per item, which Isaak said was harsher than his mother's curfew.

The test worked almost too well. When Isaak tried to launch into a speech about penguins during rocket design, Tristan pointed at the paper, and the whole room went quiet with the terrible power of a numbered list. But then Sofie noticed something sneaky. Every time they finished an item early, Tristan let it slide back open, and the mascot debate was quietly eating the budget time like erosion eating a hillside, a little at a time until the hill was gone. "You're the problem," Sofie said, grinning. "You love penguins."

"I do not," said Tristan, and then he drew a tiny penguin in the margin, which rather ruined his defence. He crossed out the doodle, wrote DONE next to the mascot item, and moved the marker to budget with the solemnity of a judge.

By Friday they had a plan, a penguin named Launchpad, and a rocket design made from a two-litre bottle. Tristan folded their fair application into an envelope, addressed it to the community centre, and marched it to the post box before his courage could erode. Isaak chased him halfway down the street waving a farewell pretzel.

"See you at the fair, Mr. Chairman!" Isaak shouted.

Tristan raised the envelope like a trophy and posted it.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
Hazel found the science lab door unlocked, which was strange, because Mr. Singh locked it every afternoon like clockwork. Inside, the turtle tank had been moved three inches from its usual spot on the counter, and the filter was silent. She crouched down. The plug lay on the floor, and a thin puddle had spread toward the radiator.

She found Mr. Singh in the hallway with a mop. "The filter got unplugged," she said. "The tank moved, too."

"I moved the tank to clean under it," he said. "The plug, I don't know. Perhaps the pump failed on its own."

"It was unplugged. The plug was all the way across the floor."

"Perhaps it slipped out." He wrung the mop. "Or perhaps someone pulled it. We will ask."

At lunch, Mr. Singh gathered the four students who had been in the lab last period: Hazel, Loukas, Elody, and a boy from another class. "I'm not accusing anyone," Mr. Singh said, though he was standing in front of them with his arms crossed, which undercut the message. "Just tell me what you saw."

The boy went first. "Loukas was messing with the tank. He picked it up, like, to look at the turtle."

"I never touched the tank," Loukas said. "I leaned on the counter to look at the turtle, and my elbow hit the filter cord. It made a weird noise. Then I fixed my backpack, and the tank was already back where it was."

"The tank moved later," Elody said. "I saw Mr. Singh move it during the period. He was cleaning." She turned to Hazel. "You were over by the radiator for like ten minutes. What were you doing?"

"Looking for my pencil," Hazel said. "It rolled under the shelving." She paused. "And I heard the filter stop. Before the cord even came out. Like a hiccup, then nothing."

"So it broke on its own," Loukas said, "and then the cord fell out."

"Or the cord came out," the boy said, "and Loukas is lying about the noise."

They argued in circles for five minutes. Two people couldn't both be right about the order of events, and yet each of them sounded exactly sure.

In English that afternoon, Hazel remembered a film her older sister had watched last month, a Japanese one, black and white, with everyone shouting at each other in a ruined gate. She'd looked it up afterward. Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other. Four witnesses, one crime, no two stories alike, and no judge at the end holding up the answer.

So after school, she went back to the lab alone. If the filter had died first, there would be a burned smell, or the pump would be stiff. She plugged it in. It hummed instantly, healthy and annoying. Then she checked the cord's length. It couldn't reach the spot where the plug had lain on its own; someone had carried it there, or dragged it. She measured the distance with a ruler from the supply drawer, twice, to reassure herself.

The next morning she found Mr. Singh by the mailboxes. "The pump works fine," she said. "And the cord can't fall out and land where it did. It has to be pulled."

Mr. Singh considered this. "The boy from the other class. He was near the outlet when I was cleaning. I turned my back for a moment."

"You don't know it was him."

"No," Mr. Singh admitted. "But it was not the plumbing of the situation, was it. The pump was innocent." He almost smiled. "Thank you, Hazel. And the puddle was temporary, so no harm done. Unlike the truth, which I will now go chase."

He walked off down the hallway, mop over his shoulder like a soldier's rifle, and Hazel stood there holding the ruler.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Elijah had never eaten dinner at Noam's house before, and he wanted to make a good impression. Noam's family had moved here from Malaysia last year, and tonight his grandmother was cooking, which Noam said was a big deal.

The smells hit Elijah at the door: lemongrass, coconut, something sizzling. Noam's grandmother greeted them with a slow bow, both hands pressed together, and Elijah copied it quickly, hoping he had the shape right. He noticed she took the box of dates he'd brought with her right hand only, and he filed that away.

At the table, rice and curries crowded every surface. Elijah reached for the chicken dish with his left hand, because it sat on his left, and then he stopped. Something was off, and it took him a second to see what. Noam's grandmother, Noam's father, even Noam himself, all of them were eating with their right hands only, scooping rice with their fingers of the right hand while the left sat quietly in their laps. When Noam's father passed the spinach, he used his right hand. When the grandmother refilled Elijah's glass, right hand again.

Elijah couldn't see any rule written anywhere, so he had to work it out from what he could observe. In science class, Mr. O'Brien had called this an inference, a conclusion drawn from evidence instead of from a direct answer. The evidence here was coherent, all pointing the same way, but Elijah wanted proof. He decided to simulate a mistake on purpose. He picked up the serving spoon with his left hand and offered the potatoes toward Noam's father.

The room went quiet in a small, careful way. Noam's grandmother drew a slow breath. Then Noam, grinning, reached across with his right hand and guided Elijah's arm, so the spoon settled into his father's palm from the other side.

"Right hand," Noam said quietly. "Right hand for eating, and for giving and receiving. It's respect. We do it in Malaysia, and Indonesia too."

Elijah switched hands. "Sorry. I didn't know."

"It's why I keep my left hand under the table," Noam whispered. "Watch my grandmother. She never lets it near the food."

Elijah watched her for the rest of the meal. She lifted the teapot with her right, took the dates back from the shelf with her right, pressed her right palm flat when she thanked him for the gift. He copied every move, and by the time the mango slices came around, his left hand had learned to stay still.

At the door, Noam's grandmother handed Elijah a container of leftovers. He received it with both hands, but he made sure his right was the one on top.

"Come again," she said, and her eyes crinkled.

Elijah carried the container home with his right hand the whole way.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
The gallery was giving a free sketching afternoon, and Beatrice had signed up with one clear ambition: to draw a street that looked like a street, not like a pile of buildings having a bad day. She sat on a bench near the big window with Dania on one side and Arno on the other, each of them with a clipboard, a pencil, and a postcard of a city street to copy.

Mr. Mercado, the gallery's education coordinator, had given them exactly one hint before wandering off to refill the coffee cups. "Find your vanishing point," he had said, "and let the sides of the buildings run toward it." Beatrice had nodded like someone who knew what that meant, then drawn a dot in the middle of her page and started.

Her first attempt went badly in a way she couldn't quite name. She had slanted the rooflines toward the dot, which looked right, and slanted the doorframes toward the dot too, and slanted the window tops and the shop signs and the shelf inside the bakery window. When she held the page up, the whole street appeared to be tipping over sideways, like every building had agreed to lean the same direction at the same moment.

"Yours looks dizzy," Arno said, leaning over. He held up his own drawing, which had no vanishing point at all and resembled a street viewed by a fly with commitment issues. Dania's was somewhere in the middle, which she claimed was a style.

Beatrice looked past her drawing to the actual window. Across the street there was a real building, facing her squarely, with real windows, and she noticed something she had never thought about before. The tops of those windows were flat. Not tilted, not aimed anywhere. Flat across, like the horizon, and the sides of them went straight up and down. She squinted at the building next door, and its window tops were horizontal too.

She modified her drawing line by line, redrawing every window top and every doorframe on the front-facing shops so they were perfectly horizontal or perfectly vertical, while keeping only the receding edges, the sides of the buildings running away from her, angled toward the dot. It felt wrong, like she was ignoring the rule, but when she held the page up again the street stood still. The buildings had stopped falling over. She checked it twice, because it seemed too easy, but there it was.

"Wait," Dania said, staring at Beatrice's page and then at her own. "You only slanted some of them."

"The ones going away from me," Beatrice said. "The ones facing me stay flat."

Arno tried it on his drawing and got the equivalent result with less charm, since his bakery now stood upright but had the proportions of a gymnasium. "Mine's still terrible," he said with visible satisfaction, "but it's terrible in a much more professional way."

Mr. Mercado drifted back with the coffee pot and looked over their shoulders. He studied Beatrice's drawing for a long moment, then studied her. "You figured that out from the window?"

"From the building across the street," Beatrice said.

He nodded slowly and moved on to Dania, and Beatrice bent back over her page, adding a bicycle leaning against the bakery's perfectly vertical door.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A climate graph usually shows each month's average temperature as a line and each month's average rainfall as bars on the same chart.
story:
The rain started just as Mr. Sharma handed out the worksheets, which Tristan took as a personal insult. "Before the bus leaves at noon," Mr. Sharma said, "each of you brings me one page: a climate graph for the Sonoran Desert and one for the Hoh Rainforest, plus three sentences comparing them." Tristan stared at the packet. The bus would leave in two hours, his tent was leaking, and he had no idea what a climate graph was.

He spread the pages on the picnic table under the tarp while Alivia and Samson argued about whose fault the leaking tent was. The first graph showed twelve tall columns with a thin line curving over the top. Tristan squinted at the columns. Those had to be temperature, obviously, because they were the biggest thing on the chart. The desert one had tiny stubs and the rainforest one had towers. "So the rainforest is hotter," he announced. "Way hotter. Look at those bars."

Samson leaned over his shoulder. "Why would the desert have almost nothing, then? It's supposed to be blazing."

"Because it's, um. Seasonal." Tristan said this with the confidence of someone who had just invented the word.

Alivia took the page from him and turned it upside down, as though that might help. It didn't, but the legend at the bottom did. "It says millimetres," she said, pointing. "Rainfall's in millimetres. So the bars are rainfall." She traced the line with her finger. "And temperature's the line, in degrees. It's all on the same chart, one month at a time, the average for each."

Tristan felt his ears go hot, which was at least thematically appropriate. He had spent ten minutes confidently reading the chart wrong. His dilemma now was simple: admit it and redo his three sentences, or hand in nonsense and hope Mr. Sharma had graded thirty worksheets already and was too tired to notice. He looked at his watch. Eleven fifteen.

Whether the Hoh was "wetter" felt subjective when you looked at numbers, so he decided to convert the idea into something nobody could argue with: the rainforest's bars stood ten times taller, and the desert's temperature line rode higher. He wrote his three sentences fast, muttering each one out loud while Samson timed him, and jogged through the mud to Mr. Sharma at the check-in table.

Mr. Sharma read the page, nodded, and handed it back. "Good work. You've got the desert hot and dry, rainforest mild and soaked." He smiled. "Shame about the worksheet, though. That one was for next month's unit. This morning's was the constellations quiz, due in ten minutes."

Samson was already holding up the second packet, waving it from under the tarp.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are considered among the safest investments in the world.
story:
Alex sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a worksheet that refused to cooperate. Ms. Tang wanted one paragraph by Monday: compare a stock and a bond, and say which is riskier and why. He had written three opening sentences already, and crumpled all three.

"Grandma," he called toward the living room, "do you own any stocks?"

She came in carrying a mug of tea and sat down across from him. "A few. Why?"

"I have to explain which is riskier, a stock or a bond, and I keep going in circles. I thought you'd say stocks, because they go up and down all the time."

"I do say stocks." She turned his worksheet sideways, reading it. "But you can't just declare it. Ms. Tang will want you to cite a reason."

Alex stared at the sugar bowl. "A stock is a piece of a company, right? So if the company does badly, my piece is worth less. That part I get." He tapped his pencil. "But a bond is just a promise. Why would anyone trust a promise?"

Grandma didn't answer. Instead she asked, "Who would you rather lend your lunch money to, Taha or some kid you've never met?"

"Taha. I know him."

"And if Taha forgot it, what would happen?"

"He'd pay me back the next day. He's never not paid anybody back." Alex stopped. "So it matters who's making the promise." He thought about his own allowance, split between a video game fund and emergency quarters taped inside his backpack. "Wait. Where do you keep your emergency savings? Not in stocks?"

"No. In Treasury bonds. They're backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, and they're considered among the safest investments in the world."

Alex wrote the line down word for word. "The whole government? Standing behind Grandma's savings?" He tested the idea out loud. "If a company breaks its promise, I lose my money. But a bond from the government is a promise from the country itself. That's why the bond is safer. The riskier one is the stock, because nobody stands behind it but the company."

"Now you have your paragraph," Grandma said, and rinsed her mug.

That evening Alex called Taha and read him the draft. Taha said the part about "full faith and credit" sounded made up, so Alex looked it up and read it back to him exactly as written. Then Braxton, who wanted to argue that picking anything was arbitrary, challenged him over the phone. "You could just as easily say stocks are safer."

"You couldn't," Alex said. "Try this. Who backs Braxton's Lemonade Incorporated?"

"Me, obviously."

"And who backs a Treasury bond?"

Braxton was quiet for a second. "Oh. Okay, that's actually a good one."

Alex hung up, smoothed the worksheet flat on his grandfather's table, and wrote his final sentence beneath the lamp.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
Chase needed to prove that his neighbor's tomato plants were dying because of the fertilizer the hardware store sold, not because he had forgotten to water them. He had a summer of allowance riding on this. His dad had made him a deal: find real evidence, and the money for new plants was his; fail, and Chase paid for the tomatoes out of his own pocket. He'd overheard a guy at the store swearing the fertilizer had saved his whole garden, one guy, one story, and Chase wanted to use it. Instead, at the library, he found a thick journal with a study on fertilizers and tomato blight, shelved right next to a printed blog post with almost the same title.

Roman was already at their usual table, balancing a pencil on his nose. "You look like a detective in a movie," he said, and the pencil fell.

"Look at this." Chase dropped both papers in front of him. "The blog is some guy saying this fertilizer wrecked his tomatoes. The journal says the same thing, but it's got all these charts and a page of numbers at the back."

Ari slid into the third chair, out of breath from racing over. She picked up the journal article and squinted at it. "There's a whole section here about how they tested it on like a zillion plants. And look, it says the paper was reviewed before publication."

"What's that mean, they liked it?" Roman asked.

"Before it went in the journal, other experts checked it for errors," Ari said. "It's called peer review."

"So the blog guy," Chase said slowly, turning both pages face up, "nobody checked him. He could've planted them upside down."

Ari grinned. "Maybe he watered them with soda."

Chase tried to categorize what he had. One story about one person's garden, which felt convincing because it was vivid, he could practically smell that guy's dead tomatoes. And one tested claim, checked by people who knew what errors looked like. He'd come in ready to argue from the story. Now he wasn't so sure the fertilizer was the villain at all. He flipped back to the journal's charts, hunting for what else might kill tomatoes.

"Here," he said, tapping a line. "Too much water does the exact same thing. Brown spots, droopy leaves." He felt his stomach drop. He had watered those plants every single day. Twice on the hot ones.

Roman raised his eyebrows. "So it might be you."

"It might be me." Chase copied the watering numbers into his notebook, then, after a moment, the fertilizer ones too. The evidence pointed both ways, and only one of them got him out of paying. "I'm going to run an experiment. Two plants, same fertilizer, different water. One's going to live."

"Cool," Ari said. "Can I be in charge of naming them?"

The librarian appeared behind them and cleared her throat, pointing at the sign that said QUIET STUDY. Roman whispered, "Fine. I declare a truce with the pencil," and set it down gently, like it might explode. Chase slid the journal into his backpack, the heaviest thing in there by far, and headed for the door to go measure his neighbor's hose.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element.
story:
Brooke stood in front of the giant periodic table wall at the science fair with her quiz sheet clutched in one hand. Question seven read: how many protons are in a neon atom? She had skipped it twice already, and now there were only ten minutes left before the answers were collected at the front desk.

"You're staring at that wall like it owes you money," said Livia, sliding up beside her.

"I don't get it. It's just a grid of boxes. Neon, neon, where's neon." She scanned the columns. The wall had to be fifteen feet wide, and every box held a symbol, a name, and a small number in the top corner. "It's not even in order alphabetically."

Livia pointed at the tiny card bolted under the display. "Read that."

Brooke leaned in. The card said that an element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element. She read it twice, then looked up at the wall with new eyes. "Wait. So the number isn't random. It's not just a label somebody made up to quantify the collection or something. It actually tells you something."

"That's what it says," Livia said.

"So if I find neon's box, the number in the corner is the answer. Not a hint, the answer." Brooke ran her finger along the top row, then the second. The boxes were numbered left to right, one, two, three, climbing as they went. She had assumed the numbers were like page numbers, a filing system. Now she thought maybe she'd had a bias against the whole table, deciding it was boring decoration before she'd actually read anything.

"Third row," said Livia. "Tenth box. Right there."

Neon, Ne, and in the corner, the number 10. Brooke checked the neighbouring boxes to test her idea. Sodium was 11, magnesium 12, aluminium 13, marching up in order. If the atomic number counted protons, then a sodium atom had one more proton than a neon atom, every single time, in every atom anywhere. She couldn't see a proton, couldn't hold one, but the pattern held all the way across the row like a code hidden in plain sight.

She wrote 10 on her sheet and underlined it. On question eight she didn't even hesitate. Gold, Au, atomic number 79. Seventy-nine protons, in every gold atom in every ring in every shop in the city.

Christine waved from the front desk. "Two minutes, people! Bring your sheets up!"

Brooke ran, sheet flapping, and slapped it down on the stack. "Number seven," she told Christine breathlessly. "Neon. Ten protons."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: A basic twelve-bar blues uses three chords, built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale and written as the I, IV and V chords.
story:
Maria had the garage to herself on Saturday afternoon, her dad's old amp humming in the corner beside a workbench covered in guitar cables. She plugged in and played the chord progression Ms. Holloway had written on the whiteboard at jazz club: twelve bars, the same three chords over and over. The trouble was the soloing. Every time the chords changed, her notes sounded like she had wandered into the wrong room.

Neveah arrived first, dragging her keyboard, then Denzel with a snare drum under one arm. "I invited Theo," Neveah said. "He plays bass, and he's actually good."

"Great," Maria said, though she had been hoping to keep the garage band a small guild of just the three of them. A bass player would hear every wrong note she played.

Theo showed up, tuned quickly, and squinted at the chart on the music stand. "What does one-four-five mean?" he asked. "Everybody keeps saying it."

Maria opened her mouth and then closed it, because she realized she did not actually know. "It's on the chart," she said, pointing at the Roman numerals. "I, IV, V. I just play them where they're written."

That bugged her all through the first run-through. While Denzel worked on his drum throne and Neveah fiddled with a patch cable, Maria sat on an overturned milk crate with her guitar unplugged. She counted up the scale from the first note. The first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale, she noticed, were exactly the roots of the three chords on the chart. That was why they were called the I, the IV, and the V. It was not random at all. It was a pattern hiding underneath every blues song she had ever heard, and she had been playing it for weeks without seeing it.

"I think I've got it," she said. "One-four-five. The chords are built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale. That's the whole system."

"So it's the same in every key?" Neveah asked.

Maria grabbed the chart, moved everything to the key of E, and counted again. Same shape, same three chords, just starting from a different note. She plugged back in. "Denzel, count it off."

They played, and this time when the chords rolled around, Maria stopped guessing. She isolated each chord change in her head, matched one safe note to it, then bent the next note and let it cry. Denzel whooped mid-fill. Even Theo nodded at her from behind the bass.

"Again," Maria said, already dialing up the volume. "Faster this time."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis points in the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and later leans away.
story:
The old quarry was flooded now, a green pool filling the pit where the machines had once chewed out limestone, and Mr. Russo had brought his science club to the flat shelf of rock at the edge so they could see something bigger than a classroom. Juliette carried the globe, Shaun carried the camping lantern, and Finnigan carried a bag of markers because he said you could not do science without drawing on something. The problem was simple and terrible: in three days Juliette had to explain the seasons to Mr. Russo's substitute, out loud, for a grade, and every time she tried, her explanation fell apart halfway through.

"Distance," Shaun said, setting the lantern on a flat stone. "Summer is when Earth is closer to the Sun. That's my guess."

"It's wrong," Juliette said. "Mr. Russo said so last week. It's something about the tilt. But then I said the tilt, and he said, okay, explain it, and I just stood there." Wind moved across the quarry water, and the surface went turbulent for a moment, choppy and gray, then smoothed out again.

She set the globe on the rock and switched on the lantern. "Okay, the lamp is the Sun. Walk the globe around it." Finnigan picked it up and started the orbit, and Juliette watched, frowning, because something was bothering her. Every quarter of the way around, Finnigan turned the globe so it faced the lamp, the way you would naturally turn anything you were carrying past a light, and she suddenly saw it.

"Stop. Stop stop stop." She held up a hand. "You keep turning it. Don't."

"I'm keeping it facing the Sun," Finnigan said. "That's good, isn't it? Facing the Sun is warm."

"No, because that's not what Earth does. The axis points the same direction in space all year." She took the globe from him and held it tilted, then walked it slowly around the lantern herself, keeping the top of the tilt aimed at the same distant point, the far rim of the quarry where an old crane still stood rusting. She aimed the north end at the crane and walked. "Look. Watch which half leans toward the lamp."

Shaun crouched down, chin nearly on the rock. When the globe was on one side of the lantern, the top half leaned in toward the light, and a bright glare ran across the whole northern face. Juliette kept walking, north end still aimed at the crane, and on the far side of the lamp the top half leaned away, its north lit at a slant, thin and pale. "Now the Northern Hemisphere is leaning away," she said. "So for part of the orbit the north leans toward the Sun, and later it leans away. Same tilt. The axis never changes direction. We just move around."

"That's it?" Finnigan said. "That's the whole secret?"

"That's the whole secret. And when the north leans toward, that's our summer. When it leans away, winter." She felt like laughing. "Shaun, your turn. Walk it. Aim the north at the crane the whole way."

Shaun did it, slow and careful, and Juliette narrated. "Leaning toward. Leaning away. Leaning toward again." Finnigan got out the markers and drew a big diagram on the flat rock: a lamp, a ring of circles, arrows showing the tilt aimed at one fixed spot. "This is our algorithm," he said. "Orbit, keep the axis pointed at the crane, announce the season. Step by step, every time."

They ran it four more times, taking turns, and by the fourth lap Shaun could do it without being reminded. When it was Juliette's turn again, she did the whole walk and the whole explanation out loud, from start to finish, the way she would have to do it for the substitute, and nobody interrupted her once. The afternoon sun was dropping behind the quarry rim, and the water below had gone calm and green again.

"One more time," she said, picking up the globe. "Somebody be the crane."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself.
story:
Rosalie had typed the same line four times, and the laptop in the camp's craft cabin kept spitting back red errors like a dragon with a cold. Around her, the coding club was supposed to be building programs that tested whether a number was prime, but so far the only thing anyone had tested was Mohamed-Amine's patience.

"I'm telling you, nine is prime," Mohamed-Amine insisted, leaning across the table. "You can't split nine into anything. Try it. Three times..." He stopped, frowned, and started over. "Okay, but listen, my point stands in spirit."

"It does not stand in anything," said Mathieu, who wanted more than anything to finish first so he could retire his reputation as the slowest typer in the club. Last summer, his flash drive had died with his only copy of a dinosaur game on it, and people still brought it up at lunch. "Nine divides by three. Three times three. It's not prime. A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself. That's the whole rule."

Rosalie ignored both of them and stared at her screen, where her loop sat half-finished and stubbornly opaque to her. She remembered, suddenly, being eight years old at her grandmother's kitchen table, dividing candies into equal rows to see which piles couldn't be arranged in neat rectangles. Eleven candies had refused every arrangement except one long line, and her grandmother had laughed and called it a stubborn number. That was the same idea, she realized. Her program just had to do what her hands had done: try every row size and see if anything divided evenly. And it had to start checking only at 2, and skip 1 and the number itself, because those always divided evenly and didn't count.

She wrote the loop, asked the program to print "prime" or "not prime," and then, feeling mischievous, ran a little census of the numbers from 2 to 30, printing each verdict. The screen filled up like a attendance sheet: 2 prime, 3 prime, 4 not prime, 5 prime, and so on down the list. When it reached 9, the word "not" appeared next to it.

"Ha!" Mathieu crowed, pointing at the screen so hard he nearly knocked over his lemonade. "Nine, not prime. The machine has spoken."

Mohamed-Amine squinted at the screen as if it might change its mind. Then he leaned back, arms crossed, considering. "Fine. But run it on thirteen. If your program says thirteen isn't prime, I'm going back to canoeing."

Rosalie typed thirteen, hit enter, and turned the laptop toward him so the word filled the screen: prime.

"Okay," Mohamed-Amine said slowly. "Now do a thousand."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Elijah had Mr. Toussaint's history project spread across the kitchen table: a photocopied page from a settler's diary, a blank poster board, and a pile of glue sticks going nowhere. The assignment said to use a primary source, an actual document from the time, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary belonged to a man named Henry, who had crossed the plains with his wife and two oxen named Bill and Bob. So far Elijah had written one sentence on the poster: "They wanted land." It felt thin.

His friend Moshe came over after school and dropped his backpack on a chair. "Still stuck?"

"Every line is about mud and broken wheels," Elijah said. He slid the page across. "Listen to this part. Henry writes that at Fort Laramie the grass was gone from thousands of wagons passing, and men kept asking each other about California."

Moshe read it twice. "Asking about California what?"

Elijah tapped the next line. "Right here. He says his cousin had 'caught the gold fever' and turned off the trail toward Sutter's Mill." He sat back. "I thought they all came for farms. Henry did. But his cousin didn't."

"So write both reasons," Moshe said.

"Mr. Toussaint wants evidence, not just my guess." Elijah pulled out his phone and searched, scrolling fast while Moshe made a prototype heading for the poster out of a torn strip of paper, moving it around to see where it looked best. "Okay. Here. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848. It started the California Gold Rush, and people headed west in huge numbers." He checked the diary page again. "Henry started out in the spring of 1849. That's after. His cousin heard about the gold and left the farm behind."

"That's your hidden cause," Moshe said. "It's not written on the page, it's under it."

Elijah grabbed a marker. He drew a simple timeline across the top of the poster, then wrote the date in careful letters. He was working faster now, and the project seemed to accelerate on its own, quotes going up, the sentence about land growing into two paragraphs, one for farmers like Henry and one for fever-driven travelers like the cousin.

His mother came by with sandwiches and stretched the poster flat with an elastic band to keep the edges from curling while the glue dried. "That looks like something," she said.

Monday, Mr. Toussaint paused at Elijah's poster longer than at any other. He read the diary quote, then the timeline. "So some came for soil and some came for gold," Elijah said, holding his breath.

Mr. Toussaint nodded and wrote something on his clipboard. "You used the source to prove it, not just to decorate. That's the whole skill."

Moshe, two desks over, gave him a thumbs up, and Elijah grinned down at Henry's muddy, golden, well-used words.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
The arena sat at the edge of the park, and behind its wide glass doors the ice gleamed white under the lights, but Livia wasn't there for hockey. Behind the rink, a cracked rubber track looped through the trees, exactly four hundred metres around, and that was where she spent every Tuesday while her little brother's practice roared on inside. Today Ameer and Auguste had come with her, and Ms. Sow, who coached the neighbourhood running group, had agreed to time them.

"Eight hundred metres," Ameer read off the clipboard. "That's two laps, right? The track's four hundred, so we go around twice." He bounced on his toes at the start line while Ms. Sow raised her stopwatch.

Livia had a problem, and it had a shape she could feel but not see. Every time she raced Ameer, she exploded off the line, flew the first lap, and then her legs turned to wet rope halfway through the second. He always caught her at the end. Something invisible was being spent, she reasoned, like money leaking out of a pocket she couldn't check. She couldn't watch it go, but she could monitor it another way, by checking her breathing and the heaviness in her calves, the way her mom watched the fuel gauge instead of staring into the gas tank.

Ms. Sow's whistle blew. Livia went out fast, and Ameer went faster, tearing ahead like the race was half as long as it was. Halfway through the first lap, she forced herself to ease back until her breathing settled into a rhythm she could hold. Ameer disappeared around the far curve. "Come on!" Auguste shouted from the infield.

Then, coming into the second lap, Ameer suddenly sprinted, arms pumping, driving for the line. Except the line wasn't there. He crossed the lap marker, slowed to a triumphant jog, and threw both arms up just as Livia and Auguste pounded past him. "It's two laps!" Auguste yelled over her shoulder. "You've still got a whole lap!" Ameer stood frozen, staring at the curve ahead, and Livia understood: he'd counted one lap as the whole race. Four hundred metres, twice. She had one lap left too, but unlike every other Tuesday, she had something still in her legs.

She dug in. Her calves burned and her lungs scraped, but the burn arrived late enough that she could fight it, and she crossed the finish two strides ahead of Auguste with Ameer stumbling in behind them, groaning about robbery.

That night he sent her a message: "You only won because I burned everything on lap one. Rematch Saturday. I'm pacing this time." Livia grinned and typed back, "Good. Bring your whole second lap." She laced her shoes by the door where she could see them, ready for morning.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Victoria had one job this afternoon: post the team photo, the one where everyone was grinning on Ms. Santos-Reyes's front porch after the robotics win. She pulled her chair up to the computer, plugged in her phone, and clicked through the pictures until she found it.

"Wait," she said to herself, leaning closer. She zoomed in on the porch steps. Behind Sophie's elbow, sharp in the sunlight, stood the house number, and just past Musa's shoulder the street sign said Maple Court. Anybody who looked at this photo could work out exactly where Ms. Santos-Reyes lived. Sophie had sent her a message about it an hour ago, and Victoria scrolled back to read it again.

"Check the background before you post," Sophie had written. "Musa spotted the sign in the corner."

"Are you serious?" Victoria had typed back.

"Dead serious," came the reply. "Musa says a stranger can zoom in just like we do. He tested it on some photo from the internet and figured out the school in, like, two minutes."

Now Victoria sat with her hand on the mouse, cursor hovering over Post. It was a great picture. Six smiling faces, the trophy, Musa holding the robot like a proud ambassador for the whole team. She wanted her followers to see it. But she kept picturing some stranger zooming in, reading the house number, reading the street sign, and knowing the porch where her friends were standing.

She tested it, the way Musa had. She opened one of her own older posts, a selfie from the school parking lot, and zoomed in until she could read the school logo on the sign by the door. It took her about ninety seconds to confirm the address online. Her stomach did a small, cold flip. It worked. Anyone could do this.

"Okay," she said out loud. She emailed Sophie and Musa, attaching the photo. "What if we crop it? Here's my idea. I cut the picture just inside the railing so the number and the sign are gone."

Musa answered within minutes. "Try it. Send the test version."

Victoria cropped, saved, and sent it back. Sophie wrote, "Zoomed in three times. Nothing. Post that one."

Before she posted it, Victoria scrolled through her other recent photos and found two more with street signs or numbers in the frame. She deleted those posts, even the one with eighty likes, which stung a little. Eighty likes were temporary anyway, she figured; the internet was forever. She had learned that much today.

Ms. Santos-Reyes saw the cropped photo that evening and sent a short reply. "Smart edit, Victoria. The team looks wonderful. Do this for every photo from now on, and I'll put you in charge of the club page."

Victoria grinned and opened a new folder on her desktop, labeled it Practice Posts, and dragged the cropped picture in first. "Every single one," she muttered, and started on the next.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
Penelope stared at the onion on her cutting board like it was a bomb. The board slid toward the edge of the counter the moment she set her knife on it, and that was the third time in ten minutes.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Mr. Murphy said from the front of the room, holding up his own hand so everyone could see the knuckles leading and the fingertips tucked safely away. "The knuckle guides the blade. The fingertips stay out of trouble."

Eddy, at the next station, was already halfway through his onion, though his pieces were approximately the size of gravel. Romain had given up and was watching the clock. Penelope put her left hand on top of the board to hold it, curled her right fingers into the claw grip the way Mr. Murphy had shown, and pressed down. The board skated sideways and the knife clattered onto the counter.

She stood there for a second, thinking. The board only slid when she pushed down hard. It never moved when she was just holding the onion still. So the problem wasn't the board itself, it was something between the board and the counter, something she couldn't see, letting it slip. She wiped the counter with a paper towel, then wrung the towel out and spread it flat under the board before anyone could tell her it was a weird thing to do. She pressed down. The board held still, like it was glued.

"Did you just put a wet towel under there?" Eddy asked, leaning over.

"A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding while you chop," she said, and demonstrated with a firm push. Nothing moved. "Wet paper towel under the board. It stays put."

By the end of class she had a pile of even onion pieces sweating into the pan, olive oil popping softly around them, and the beginnings of a real sauce. Mr. Murphy wandered by, took one look at the board, and nodded. Romain, watching from his empty station, quietly got up, dampened a paper towel, and slid it under his own board.

"Smell that," Eddy said as the onions turned golden.

Penelope turned down the burner and smiled. "Dinner," she said.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: An "upstander" is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander.
story:
John had watched the whole thing happen at lunch on Thursday and had not said a word. Some kids in the next row had taken Dominik's drawing and passed it around, calling it baby art, and John had kept eating his sandwich while Dominik sat there with his ears going red. That afternoon, in Ms. Li's class, they had talked about it. "An upstander," Ms. Li had said, "is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander." She hadn't looked at John, but the words landed on him anyway. Watching was exactly what he had done.

All weekend at his grandpa's house, the word followed him around. On Saturday he helped his grandpa sand an old wooden vessel in the shed, a rowboat they were fixing up together, and his grandpa said, "You're diligent today," which was true, but only because sanding kept his hands busy while his mind worked. He kept testing ideas in his head. If he yelled at the kids, that would make it worse, because then it would become a fight and Dominik would be in the middle of it. If he told a teacher, Dominik might get called a snitch. There had to be a third thing.

On Sunday his friend Thiago came over, and John asked him to run through it in the shed. "Pretend you just grabbed Dominik's drawing," John said. "Say something mean about it."

Thiago held up a rag like it was a picture. "This is baby art."

"Okay, and I say..." John stopped. "Hand it back." He tried it plain, no anger, just like handing back a dropped pencil. "Hey, hand it back. It's his." Thiago passed the rag over, and John realized something: he hadn't insulted anyone. He hadn't even said the teasing was wrong out loud. He had just made the normal thing happen, quietly, like a door swinging back into place.

On Monday the same kids were at it again, spinning Dominik's notebook out of reach. John's stomach tightened, but he walked over and said, "Give it back. It's his," and held out his hand, the way he'd practiced between the sawhorses. The kid holding the notebook glanced around, seemed to lose interest without anything to push against, and dropped it on the table. Dominik pulled it close and went back to his drawing, and for a second his eyes met John's.

After school, Dominik caught up with him at the corner by the fence. "Thanks," he said. "You didn't have to do that."

John shrugged, feeling his ears go warm. "It's called being an upstander," he said. "I looked it up."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
Victoria spread her catapult across the big table by the library window, wedged between the atlas shelf and a kid who was supposed to be doing homework. The science fair was in nine days, and her poster board sat empty except for a title: "Which Angle Launches Farthest?" She had built the catapult from a kit, but it wasn't behaving.

"The sixty-degree launch just went four meters," she told Samara, who had come to help in exchange for borrowing Victoria's colored markers for her own project. "Yesterday at the same angle it barely went two. I can't put that on a poster. It makes no sense."

Samara leaned over the measuring tape they had stretched along the carpet. "Maybe something's loose. Did you check the arm?"

"Twice." Victoria fired again, and the pom-pom sailed past the end of the tape entirely, bounced off a book cart, and rolled under the biography section. A man at the next table looked up. Mr. Campbell-Brown, the librarian, raised one eyebrow. Victoria mouthed "sorry" and retrieved her projectile.

She sat down and stared at her one data point. Then she thought about the poster itself. A single launch wasn't a measurement, really. It was one moment, with who knew what wobbling through it. She pulled a fresh sheet of paper and wrote "60 degrees" at the top, then drew ten blank lines beneath it. "One weird launch is an anomaly," she said, mostly to herself. "If I do it a bunch of times and take the average, a bad throw shouldn't ruin everything." Samara nodded slowly and offered to record while Victoria fired.

They ran ten launches at sixty degrees, then ten at forty-five, then ten at thirty. The pom-pom still scattered, short hops and wild heaves, but the averages settled down: forty-five degrees won by more than half a meter. When Mr. Campbell-Brown wandered over to see what they were doing, Victoria showed him the table of numbers. He studied it longer than she expected. "So the conventional approach would be one careful shot per angle," he said. "You did better than that."

"Mostly by accident," Victoria admitted.

"That's how most science works," he said, and went back to his cart.

Samara spent the last hour copying the results into neat bar graphs while Victoria lettered the conclusion: repeating each trial ten times and averaging the results gave numbers she could trust. The scatter was still there in the raw data, plain on the page, but it no longer felt like the project failing. It felt like the project working. Samara capped the last marker and held up her own graph of the school's recycling bins, counted twice.

"Same trick," Samara said. "Count it ten times, average it, and my numbers stop arguing with each other."

"Then let's count them again," Victoria said, and pulled the tape measure back to the start of the carpet.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
"Before you go, what's the address here?" Abigail asked, holding her pencil over the pad next to the phone. "The whole thing, with the number."

Ms. Holloway paused with her coat half on. "Fourteen Sycamore Court. Why do you need that?"

"My mom says if you ever have to call for help, the emergency dispatcher usually asks for the address of the emergency first, before anything else. So a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they're in." Abigail wrote it in careful letters and underlined it. "Just in case."

Ms. Holloway smiled, kissed her son Marcus on the head, and said she'd be back by nine. Then the door closed, and the house went quiet in a way that felt bigger than it had five minutes ago.

Marcus was two, and he had a bedtime ritual that Abigail had memorized from the note on the fridge: one story, one song, water in the blue cup and not the green one, and the night-light with the whale on it. She followed every step like a recipe, and by eight he was asleep, one arm flung over his stuffed rabbit. She sat in the hallway outside his room and texted Myah about how well it was going.

Then she heard it, a sound like a small engine trying to start, a dry coughing from behind his door. She went in. Marcus was sitting up, and each breath pulled in fast and whistled out slow, and his shoulders were working harder than they should. Abigail remembered, suddenly and clearly, the day in fourth grade when Yaseen had an asthma attack in gym class and the coach had stood frozen until the nurse came. She had decided then, walking home, that she would never be the person who froze.

She grabbed the pad by the phone, where FOURTEEN SYCAMORE COURT waited under its underline, and dialed. The dispatcher's voice came on, calm and quick, and the first thing she asked was exactly what Abigail had written down. "Fourteen Sycamore Court," Abigail said, and it came out steady, and she felt her fear shrink to something proportional to what she could actually do, which was give information and hold Marcus's hand. She said his age, said he was struggling to breathe, said his parents were out until nine. She kept her eyes on the whale night-light, which cast its slow blue circle on the wall, transforming the ordinary ceiling into something like an ocean, while Marcus leaned against her arm and breathed, and breathed, and somewhere down the street a siren began.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
Aria set the shoebox on the kitchen table and peeled the tape slowly, the way you open something you want to remember. Inside, on a nest of tissue paper, sat her first phone. Her mom had said she could have it if she promised to be careful, and Aria had promised before her mom even finished the sentence.

"Set it up while I make dinner," her mom said, chopping onions at the counter. The kitchen smelled sharp and sweet at the same time, and outside the window the sky had gone the gray that usually meant precipitation by morning.

Aria turned the phone over in her hands. It felt lighter than she expected, like it was barely there at all. She chose a passcode, added her name, and texted Giselle just to see the little word "delivered" appear under the bubble. Giselle replied in three seconds with fourteen exclamation points.

Then the phone buzzed with something else. A message from an app she barely used, one she'd made an account on months ago at Salome's house. "Your login code is 482013," it said. "Enter this code to sign in."

Aria frowned at it. She hadn't tried to sign in. She hadn't touched that app in weeks. So why was it sending her a code? She sat very still, the way she did when a math problem looked easy but wasn't. Somewhere, she thought, someone was typing her password. The code was like a doorbell ringing when she hadn't rung it. Somebody's finger was on her button.

She texted Salome. "Did you try to log into my account?"

"Nope, why?"

Aria chewed her lip. If someone had her password, then the code on her screen was the only thing standing between that stranger and her account. The password alone wasn't enough; the app wanted a second proof, and the second proof came to her phone, her pocket, her hands. What was that called? She'd heard Ms. Holloway mention it once during a technology unit, some phrase with the word "factor" in it. She searched it: two-factor authentication. That was it. She whispered the words out loud, just to hear how they fit together.

So the stranger had the first thing but not the second. She tried a small test, the way she tested ideas in science class. She tapped "forgot password" and changed the password to something long and strange, with her dog's name spelled backward and a symbol. Then she signed out on her own device and watched. A minute later, another code arrived, "Your login code is..." for an account nobody should be trying to enter. Two codes now. The pattern was holding: someone was knocking, and the knocking kept coming.

"Mom," Aria called, "I think somebody stole one of my passwords."

Her mom came over, still holding the onion knife, and read the screen. "You changed it?"

"Right away. But how did they get the old one in the first place?"

Her mom set down the knife. "Could you have used the same password somewhere else?"

Aria thought about it. The old password was the one she'd made up in fifth grade, the one she'd typed into a game site because it was easy to remember, the one she'd reused everywhere because remembering a dozen passwords felt like trying to demolish a mountain with a teaspoon. Now the mountain had crumbled from the other side.

She opened the settings and turned on the second proof for every account she had, one by one, watching each little toggle flip green like a row of porch lights coming on. She picked different passwords for each one, writing them in a notebook she labeled in careful letters.

"One more code came," she told her mom, holding up the phone. The stranger had knocked again, and again the door had stayed shut.

At the counter, the onions had gone soft and golden. Aria slid the notebook into her backpack, then looked at the phone still glowing in her hand, and wondered what else it might tell her that she hadn't asked yet.

The screen went dark, and outside, the first few drops of rain tapped against the kitchen window.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: The three points in an argument must be truly different reasons; if two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two.
story:
Vincent spread his notebook across the library table so Morgan could see the page, where he had written "Thesis: The town should build a skate plaza behind the rec center" and under it three numbered points. "Ms. Addo says we need the thesis and the outline before we draft anything," he said. Outside, a monsoon of rain hammered the tall windows, and the lights inside felt warmer because of it. "Point one, no place to skate downtown. Point two, kids keep getting kicked out of the parking garage. Point three, there's nowhere legal to skate."

Morgan pulled the notebook closer and read it twice, tapping the numbers with a pencil. "Points two and three are the same reason wearing different clothes. Getting kicked out of the garage and having nowhere legal, that's both just 'no place to skate.' If two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two."

Vincent leaned back and stared at the fluorescent lights. He thought about last spring, when he had written a whole essay about why his old dog was the best dog, and Ms. Addo had circled two paragraphs and written "repetition" in green ink. He'd been annoyed then, and had told himself she just didn't like him. Now he wondered whether she had seen something he hadn't. He envied Morgan a little, the way the outlines came apart in her hands like a diagram, every piece labeled. "Okay," he said slowly. "So I need a third point that's a different reason."

"Like money," Morgan said. "A plaza brings skaters from other towns, they buy food, the shops like it. That's not about where you skate. That's about why the town benefits."

Vinett crossed out his point three, and a buoyant feeling lifted his chest, the same one he got when a trick finally landed after weeks of falling. He wrote "attracts visitors who spend money at nearby shops" and then, because he couldn't stop, added a fourth line: "keeps kids active after school." "Four's too many," Morgan said. "Pick three." He looked at them, all four reasons sitting there, each one truly different, and chose.

He carried the notebook to the front desk where Ms. Addo was checking in a stack of returns. She read the page, and her eyebrows went up. "Three points, three separate reasons," she said. "You may start drafting." Vincent walked back past the rain-streaked windows and opened to a clean page. "The town should build a skate plaza behind the rec center," he wrote, "because there is nowhere legal to skate downtown, the plaza would attract visitors who spend money at nearby shops, and it would keep kids active after school."

Morgan read it over his shoulder and said, "Now that's an argument."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Tyler stood at the end of the wooden dock with his duffel bag at his feet and a knot in his stomach the size of a walnut. In two hours his dad would drive him to the bus for Camp Windrow, his first summer away, and Mr. Schneider had offered one last hour on the lake. Amir and Harlyn sat on the dock edge, backs to the water, watching Tyler like he was about to perform surgery.

"You're going to a canoeing camp," Harlyn said, "and you've never been in a canoe."

"It's a regular camp with a canoeing block," Tyler said, which made it worse, not better, since he'd signed up for that block himself.

Mr. Schneider held the green canoe steady against the dock, one weathered hand on each gunwale. "Go ahead, Tyler. Step in whenever you're ready."

Tyler put his left foot on the side of the canoe, the curved edge closest to the dock, because that seemed like the obvious place. The canoe tipped instantly, hard, and cold lake water sloshed over his sneaker. He grabbed the dock, heart hammering, while Amir made a sound like a deflating balloon.

"You almost went in," Amir said. "Full clothes. Phone in your pocket."

"That's not funny." But a small resentment toward the canoe itself had already started forming in Tyler's chest, the way you can resent a door that sticks or a bike chain that comes off. It was just wood and plastic. It still seemed to be out to get him.

He crouched and studied the thing. When he pressed down on the side, it tipped. When he pressed in the middle, it barely moved. The canoe rocked around its center, he realized, the way a seesaw rocks around its middle bar, and the middle bar of a seesaw is exactly where you want to sit. "I should step into the middle," he said slowly, "not onto the side." He remembered his cousin once saying people keep their weight low and centered in a canoe, that's the whole trick, and now the words finally meant something.

"So step in the middle," Harlyn said.

"I'm interpreting the situation, thank you." Tyler put one foot, then the other, straight into the center of the canoe, crouching low like a crab, and the boat settled under him, steady as a table. He sat down on the bottom, knees bent, paddle across his lap, and let out a breath. It worked. It really worked.
